title: Field Guide to Fable
description: Anthropic's Tarik Shihipar on how to work with Fable, a new class of model. Four parts: unhobbling Claude, finding your unknowns, dealing with the grief, and being unreasonable. A summary of his AI Engineer talk.

title: Weekly 36: The Daily Stand-Up
description: Mike's new daily stand-up skill turns your morning Google Ads check into a little team of analysts: seven analysts run every campaign, then a bull-and-bear growth-vs-efficiency debate goes to a strategist for the final call, and you rate each recommendation so it learns your judgment.

title: Weekly 35: How to Make Claude Code More Useful
description: Where you put an instruction matters more than the wording. A tour of Claude Code's toolkit - CLAUDE.md for facts, skills for runbooks, rules for edges, hooks for must-always-happen, subagents for side-quests - and the three questions that pick the right one.

title: Weekly 34: Cloudflare Explained
description: The engine room behind the brain: Cloudflare holds your API keys behind a wall, gives each person their own revocable token, hosts your sites, and runs a private tunnel to your Workbench - all on the free tier.

title: Weekly 33: Loop Engineering
description: Stop prompting the work, build the loop that does it. The four questions that decide whether a loop is worth building, the four ingredients of a good one, and why you add training wheels before autopilot.

title: Weekly 32: Meet the Workbench
description: The Workbench is where Mike now spends his day: click play on any project to spawn a fresh Claude session with full context, and right-click anything to change it in about two minutes.

title: Weekly 31: AI Building Blocks: Tools, Skills, Agents and Workflows
description: Tools, Skills, Agents, Hooks, Teams and Workflows - the primitives inside Claude and when to reach for each, so you stop guessing whether something is a skill or an agent.

title: Weekly 30: Use HTML to Build Better AI
description: Before asking for an artifact, ask: am I going to consume this or edit it? If you'll consume it, ask for HTML not Markdown - real clickable, zoomable infrastructure instead of a monospaced terminal.

title: Weekly 29: Different Design Styles
description: Grab detailed 'design MD' files, drop them in a folder, and have Claude build 14 one-page proof-of-concept sites from one brief in a single session. Brilliant for client landing-page proposals.

title: Weekly 28: AgentView from Anthropic
description: Anthropic's AgentView shows every running Claude Code session on one screen with a 'needs input' flag, so parallel work stops getting buried. Handy if you run lots of sessions, less so at two or three.

title: Weekly 27: Right-Click Customization with Claude Channels
description: Claude Channels lets a background session listen to your app and rewrite its own code: right-click any element, describe the change in plain English, and Claude edits the software. The customization layer is the point.

title: Pirate Borg: Running the Dark Caribbean
description: A GM's briefing on the setting of Pirate Borg. What the Dark Caribbean is, the real Golden Age of Piracy history it's built on (Nassau's pirate republic, the sinking of Port Royal, Tortuga's buccaneers, the Spanish treasure fleets, and where the Yucatan actually is), and then the twist: the Scourge, ASH, the six-chapter apocalypse, the seven powers from the pirate republic to the Wretched cult, the vibe of each island, and what the monster list tells you about the tone. Ends with how it actually feels to run at the table.

title: Building a 10x10 Hex Map with Dice
description: Five dice-driven methods for filling a hundred hexes with terrain, settlements, dungeons and encounters, built on the Bare World and OSWR tables you already own.

title: Hex Maps Addendum: The Welsh Piper & Hex Flowers
description: Two coherent, famous methods for neighbour-dependent hex terrain: Erin Smale's Welsh Piper adjacency system and Goblin's Henchman's hex flower engine, both wired to the Bare World tables.

title: The Wrong Shadow: Building Worlds from Knave's Tables
description: A design diary on turning Knave 2E's random tables into two settings, the Saltmere and the Starscar, and a fully playable module booklet, plus the method underneath.

title: 2D6 Dungeon 1: What It Is and Why It Fits You
description: Learn 2D6 Dungeon, episode 1. What the game is, and why a roll-and-write dungeon crawler suits how you think.

title: Scarlet Heroes 1: The Lone Hero
description: Learn Scarlet Heroes, episode 1. What the game is, the problem it solves, and why a single-hero sword-and-sorcery game played as a duet with your GM fits how you want to play.

title: Scarlet Heroes 2: Making a Hero
description: Character creation start to finish. Attributes, the four classes, the Fray die, background traits, gear and descending armour class, in about ten minutes.

title: Scarlet Heroes 3: One Against Many
description: The engine that keeps a lone hero alive: the damage-conversion rule, hit dice versus hit points, the free-every-round Fray die, and Defy Death.

title: Scarlet Heroes 4: The Unseen Game Master
description: The solo and duet toolkit. The yes/no oracle, the world-building generators, and how our sessions run with fair dice rolled in the open.

title: Scarlet Heroes 5: Into the Sunset Isles
description: Our campaign. The Red Tide setting, the ruined Westmark frontier, the town of Hulun Bir, your companion, and a first night where the wells turn red.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 1: The Sunset Isles
description: A companion guide to the world of the Red Tide, in my own words. Chapter one: the drowned world, the last refuge, and the crimson mist that waits offshore.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 2: A Crimson Past
description: The history of the Sunset Isles, in my own words: the vanished dwarves, Lammach's vision, the Landing, the Bright Years, the Ravaging, and the tense present of 300 AL.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 3: Peoples - Humankind
description: The human cultures of the last refuge, in my own words: Imperials, Kueh, Eirengarders, Eshkanti, Gadaal, and Skandr - who they were, and what they cling to now.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 4: Dwarves, Elves & Halflings
description: The demihuman peoples and their strange afterlives, in my own words: the dwarves and the Mother Below, the elves and their endless recurrence, and the quietly unbreakable halflings.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 5: The Shou
description: The native enemy of the Isles, in my own words: the four breeds, the faith of Shakun, the witch-priestesses, the feuding that saves mankind, and the Shou hatred of the Tide itself.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 6: The Lay of the Land
description: The geography of the Isles, in my own words: the two great islands, the four climate bands, the deadly Wrack at the centre, the Godbarrow mountains, and the strange outer islands.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 7: State and Society
description: The powers that rule the Isles, in my own words: the Mandarinate of Xian, the pious Hohnberg Pact, the soul-cutting Magocracy of Tien Lung, the damned Shogunate, and the dwarves of Altgrimmr.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 8: Red Sorcery
description: How magic works on the Isles, in my own words: geomancy and the soul, godbone, the afterlife and hungry ghosts, the four traditions, elven sorcery, and the ever-hungry Hell Kings.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 9: A Bestiary of the Isles
description: The monsters of the Isles as a world-dweller knows them, in my own words: Isle ogres, lizardfolk and Old Sleepers, ancient constructs, infernal demons and Hell Kings, and the horrors of the Tide.

title: Red Tide Setting Guide 10: The Tide Moves Again
description: The closing chapter, in my own words: the present crisis of 300 AL - the land squeeze, the Shogun's open war, the rising Tide Cults - and why heroism on the Isles falls to small, stubborn bands.

title: The Machine Behind the Table 1: The Ceiling
description: Series 2, from the system architect's chair. We did not build an AI game master - we took the game master's six jobs apart and handed each to whoever can hold it honestly. Why inventing looks exactly like competence, the forty-lines-per-table ceiling and the unbounded denominator behind it, the code-versus-data line, and why processes deliberately stayed code.

title: The Machine Behind the Table 2: Every Verb, and Where It Lives
description: The full inventory: 44 commands in six layers. The verb list is not a feature list, it is the list of decisions the AI is no longer allowed to make. Computation, draws, procedures, stateful runs, discovery, session - plus why every print has two audiences and only one of them is a reader.

title: The Machine Behind the Table 3: Processes Are Declared Code
description: Tables solved content; processes solve sequence. The six procedures, what momentum silently drops, and the moment the design was thrown out: a clockwise hex search in the wilderness rules that cannot be configuration without inventing a bad programming language. Plus why JUDGE markers locate interpretation rather than constrain it.

title: The Machine Behind the Table 4: Why Verify Is Mandatory
description: The layer with no equivalent at a human table: not trusting your own notes. Four ways a scan can lie to you in a single table, three of which look completely fine, the Japanese names that ended up on a Chinese city and were caught in play by accident, and why fair dice do not help if the table lost three entries to a wrapped line.

title: The Machine Behind the Table 5: The Designer Surface
description: The last job, and the one deliberately not automated. Two roles, one window; the system-versus-world line; distilled never transcribed; generated never authored. Closing with what all of this costs - fluency, setup, and a world that refuses to give you the scene you asked for.

title: Weekly 37: Adding Context by Dragging Files
description: How Mike feeds context into a session: screenshots pasted straight in, and files dragged into the chat (shift-drop) so the path lands in the prompt. The bit that should change how you organise your brain - dragging a file makes Claude read that folder's CLAUDE.md then walk up the tree, so the root file should hold only what belongs in every conversation.

title: Weekly 38: The Expertise Curve
description: The real skill with AI right now is how fast you can tell whether the output is any good - and that depends on the expertise you already have. Mike's curve: deep expertise makes AI a force multiplier with tight error bars, no expertise leaves error bars so wide you cannot tell what you got, and the dangerous middle is where you can judge the output but not the plan. What to do at each point, why you never let it mark its own homework, and why the curve is per task, never per person.

title: Learn Cowork 1: What is Cowork?
description: Cowork is a desktop app that works directly with the files on your computer. Not texting a smart friend, but having them sit at your desk and do the work. What it is, what you need, and why it is not a browser tab.

title: Learn Cowork 2: How It Is Different from ChatGPT
description: The copy-paste problem, and the bigger shift underneath it: ChatGPT answers questions, Cowork does tasks. A side-by-side of the two, and why they are not competing.

title: Learn Cowork 3: Installing Cowork
description: Download, install, sign in, and what you see when you land. Plus the three things that usually go wrong on a first install and how to fix each one.

title: Learn Cowork 4: The Interface Tour
description: What you see before a conversation and what appears once you start one: the Progress, folder and Context panels. The simplest mental model for the whole interface.

title: Learn Cowork 5: Giving Cowork a File
description: The two ways in - pointing it at a folder, or dragging a file into the chat - and the kinds of requests that work well once it has something to hold.

title: Learn Cowork 6: Where Your Results Go
description: Results are real files in a real folder, not chat bubbles you copy from. The simple pattern: questions get answered in chat, tasks produce files. Plus how editing and permissions work.

title: Learn Cowork 7: What Cowork Can and Cannot See
description: The boundaries. What it can reach (your folder, files you drag in, the conversation), what it cannot (other folders, your inbox, your screen), and how the permission model works.

title: Learn Cowork 8: What Is a Skill?
description: The gap between useful and exactly what I needed. A skill is a playbook that turns Cowork from a generalist into a specialist, shown through a before-and-after on the same blog post.

title: Learn Cowork 9: Installing a Skill
description: Thirty seconds, start to finish: get the zip, open Customize, upload, use it. Plus the three failure modes and how to get past them.

title: Learn Cowork 10: Skills in Action
description: Three skills and what they actually produce - Content Repurposer, Meeting Intelligence, and the CSV analysers - each shown as without-a-skill versus with-a-skill, and the pattern they all share.

title: Learn Cowork 11: Connectors and the Real World
description: Connectors link Cowork to Gmail, Calendar and Drive, which is where it stops being helpful with documents and starts running parts of your business. Start with reading, then go active.

title: Learn Cowork 12: Safety and Trust
description: What Cowork does well (everything it does shows up in the conversation) and where to be careful. Treat the output like work from a new team member, not a finished product.

title: Learn Cowork 13: Going Further
description: Where this goes next: the brain system as the engine room where skills get built, the Ads to AI community, and the three things to do right now.

title: Cowork for Scouts 1: What This Course Is and Who It Is For
description: Not a Claude Code refresher - what comes next. Taking what you have built and making it useful to people who will never open a terminal: your team, and your clients. The two audiences, and the four things you will be able to do by the end.

title: Cowork for Scouts 2: The SST Framework and Where Cowork Fits
description: Summit, Scouts, Trekkers. Why the openness that makes Claude Code powerful for you is exactly the wrong thing for a Trekker, and where Cowork sits: a task interface, not a terminal. What carries over from your skill design, and what does not.

title: Cowork for Scouts 3: What You Already Have and What Is Different
description: Skill files, context design and workflow patterns transfer. API access, scheduling, hooks and slash commands do not. An honest map of what to repackage versus rebuild, plus the compounding advantage of community-built skills.

title: Cowork for Scouts 4: What Trekkers Need vs What Scouts Need
description: Scouts need flexibility. Trekkers need a clear path to one outcome. The five marks of a skill that is ready for someone else, and the counterintuitive discipline underneath: reduce what is available, do not expand it.

title: Cowork for Scouts 5: Cowork Orientation - The Trekker View
description: A full walk of the interface through one lens: what will the person you hand this to actually see? Mode selector, working folder, skills panel, slash commands, scheduling, permissions and the two layers of instructions - each with the pre-configure tip that goes with it.

title: Cowork for Scouts 6: Setting Up Context for Someone Else
description: The five things always-on context must cover, how to gather them during discovery, and how to write for a business you have known for an hour. Plus the four ways context files go wrong - too generic, too long, missing the key rule, and never reviewed.

title: Cowork for Scouts 7: Running a Discovery Session
description: Twenty to thirty minutes to find how someone actually works. How to frame it so nobody gets defensive, the five questions, the follow-up that turns vague answers into a buildable workflow, and how to take spec notes rather than meeting notes.

title: Cowork for Scouts 8: Spotting Automatable Workflows
description: Four filters - repetitive, rule-based, text-heavy, currently manual - plus the workflows that pass, the ones that do not, an eight-point checklist, and how to redirect a client away from their favourite oversized idea without dismissing it.

title: Cowork for Scouts 9: Prioritising Where to Start
description: The first build is a trust problem, not a technical one. Score candidates on repetition and risk, start at highest repetition and lowest risk, and sequence outward from there. Plus the question to ask when you genuinely cannot choose.

title: Cowork for Scouts 10: Translating a Workflow Into a Skill File
description: The five sections every skill needs - goal, steps, tools, output format, edge cases - worked through on a post-meeting email. How much detail is too much, and the four mistakes Scouts make when building for someone else.

title: Cowork for Scouts 11: Writing for Someone Else Voice and Context
description: Voice is tone, terminology, naming and register, and none of it can be inferred - you have to ask. The questions to ask in discovery, how to embed the answers in the skill file, and what to do when the client voice is inconsistent.

title: Cowork for Scouts 12: Skills, Context, and How Trekkers Trigger Work
description: Three places instructions can live - skills, folder instructions, global instructions - and the decision rule for each. Why focused skills beat one big one, and how several skills combine without you orchestrating anything.

title: Cowork for Scouts 13: Connecting to Tools via MCP
description: MCP as a bridge between Cowork and the tools clients already use. The common agency connections, the four-step setup pattern, what to do when a client stack differs from yours, and handling API keys on least-privilege terms.

title: Cowork for Scouts 14: Scheduling - Automations That Run Themselves
description: Cowork schedules natively, with one limitation you must communicate: tasks only run while the machine is awake and the app is open. What to schedule, what to keep manual, and the four checks that prove a schedule is actually running.

title: Cowork for Scouts 15: Testing Before Anyone Touches It
description: Test as if you will not be there to explain what went wrong. Five pre-handoff tests, three more for anything scheduled, what done actually means, and why the testing log is the step you should not skip when you are in a hurry.

title: Cowork for Scouts 16: Setting Up Cowork for a Trekker
description: Make the right thing the only obvious thing. Folder structure, which three to five skills to surface, descriptions that both Claude and the Trekker can read, and the checklist that says a workspace is finished rather than in progress.

title: Cowork for Scouts 17: Onboarding Team Members
description: One demo, one task, one win - and nothing else in the first session. What not to explain, how to sequence a rollout by role rather than all at once, how to handle the sceptic, and why depth beats breadth when building the habit.

title: Cowork for Scouts 18: Maintaining and Growing the Team Skill Library
description: Your role shifts from builder to maintainer. When to add, when to retire, the four things that clutter a workspace fastest, and the one question to ask each Trekker every few weeks to surface friction they would never volunteer.

title: Cowork for Scouts 19: Setting Up Global Instructions
description: The always-on context that shapes every session. Where to find it, the three things it must cover in under 300 words, a template to adapt, how to handle per-project context, and when to review it.

title: Cowork for Scouts 20: Setting Up Cowork for a Client
description: Same tool, same build, different relationship. Structured discovery, formal access requests, a higher polish bar, changes that go through a process, and what to say when the client asks to edit skills themselves.

title: Cowork for Scouts 21: Teaching Clients to Use It
description: Your job is to make them capable, not to use it for them. A 30-minute session, making it feel easy without being condescending, addressing nervousness about AI directly, and the four things a capable client can do at the end.

title: Cowork for Scouts 22: The Demo That Creates the Moment
description: You are not explaining how Cowork works - you are creating one moment where the client thinks I need this. Set up the before, pick the right workflow, rehearse it, and then say almost nothing while it runs.

title: Cowork for Scouts 23: Iteration and Ongoing Support
description: Set the expectation before handoff so refinement feels normal rather than like a fault. The specific questions to ask two weeks in, how to translate vague feedback into a concrete change, and the language that frames every update as progress.

title: Cowork for Scouts 24: Building a Shared Skill Library
description: Every skill is a library asset first and a client deliverable second. Separating logic from context so an install takes an hour instead of a week, organising by function, versioning as you improve, and starting the library at client one.

title: Cowork for Scouts 25: The Skill Marketplace
description: Not a product catalogue - a Scout with a library of things that work and clients who trust them. How to frame a new skill as value rather than upsell, how to package for a fast install, and the ongoing touchpoint it creates.

title: Cowork for Scouts 26: Becoming the Embedded AI Partner
description: The consultant who sets it up and moves on is replaceable. The person who knows how the business thinks is not. What embedded means in practice, a monthly and quarterly structure, and why it is better for both sides.

title: Cowork for Scouts 27: The Compounding Effect
description: Library, understanding and capacity compound together and reinforce each other. What twelve months of consistent work actually looks like, why the knowledge outlasts the skills, and the one specific action to take this week.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 1: The Missing Person at the Table
description: What solo RPG oracles are actually for. Why the referee is mechanically a box holding information you don't have, what happens to play when that box is removed, and why the useful question about any oracle is not simple-vs-complex but which of the referee's ten jobs it takes over. Plus how the field got here, from 1970s solo wargaming to the 2003 arrival of dice-driven question answering.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 2: The Question, the Odds, and the Randomiser
description: The three mandatory parts. Why a dead question wastes a roll and how to test for a live one, the rule that separates world-facing unknowns from character-facing choices, why you must declare the odds before you roll rather than after, and how several dice of different colours can be read as separate channels from a single throw.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 3: The Answer Ladder
description: The most important idea in the field. Why a plain yes or no closes your question and returns the creative burden to you, how the six-rung ladder works, and why the value lives entirely in the and and the but. Includes why constraints are generative, and why not creative enough is almost always a false diagnosis.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 4: Anomalies and Interpretation
description: How a pile of tables learns to interrupt you. Doubles as a free second channel, the Recluse inversion that attacks your premise rather than your plan, and the trap inside spark tables: two species that look identical and behave in opposite ways. Plus apophenia, confirmation bias, and why oracles should be the spice and not the main course.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 5: Pacing, State Variables and the Scene Engine
description: The episode that saves campaigns. Why solo games plateau from comfort rather than lack of ideas, how one persistent number moves escalation out of your willpower and into the mechanism, and how to solve the dead end that ends more solo campaigns than anything else. Includes a ninety-second scene engine you can build yourself.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 6: Generators, and Where Continuity Comes From
description: Why generators answer what is it rather than is it so, the specialist emulator built for the one moment solo play collapses most reliably, and the composition rules that make combined tables work: four axes maximum, one question per table, and the anchor test. Then the cheapest clever mechanic in the hobby: two numbered lists that manufacture the feeling of a plot closing around you.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 7: Cards, the Randomiser With a Memory
description: A die has no memory and a deck does, and everything interesting follows from that. Depletion as inevitability with unknown timing, salting a prepared card into a random deck, removal as campaign history, and why cards laid on a table are external memory rather than something you maintain in your head. Includes the arithmetic that converts a set of thirty-six-entry tables into a thirty-six card deck.

title: The Anatomy of an Oracle 8: Aphantasia, and Designing Your Own
description: The assumption baked into almost every random table ever printed, and what happens when it does not hold. Show the symptom not the diagnosis, assembly rather than synthesis, and the insight that process and content fail differently, so you can keep a system's procedure and replace its tables. Ends with a diagnostic: match the symptom to the missing part, and the four traps that end campaigns.

title: Weekly 39: Organising Your To-Do Items
description: Mike had 70 items scattered across projects and the Workbench and couldn't tell what mattered. The fix: one home per to-do (a markdown file in the project folder), two layers per item (a headline short enough to judge at a glance, detail underneath for Claude), and a machine-readable priority line so code can sort without burning tokens. The bigger idea - use as much AI as you need and as little as you can get away with. Anything if-this-then-that should be a script.

title: Weekly 40: Graph Engineering = Work
description: The new buzzword after prompt, context and loop engineering - and Mike's verdict is that you can skip it, because it's a new name for work you're already doing. Coming up a level from doing the work to designing the system that does it: plan, research, skeptic, merge, decide. His meeting-prep skill turns out to be a graph. Where you put the check depends on what a mistake would cost, and the more you trust it the more you get out of the way.

title: Weekly 41: Why I Created Client Brain
description: The why, not the how-to. Mike's thesis: just doing Google Ads stops being enough in six to eighteen months, squeezed by client perception, Google, nervous agencies cutting price, and AI-native newcomers. The answers are get known, or add services and bundle them. Client Brain makes AI multiplayer by sharing context, skills and connectors - aimed at small businesses you already have a relationship with, starting at email triage and meeting prep. Not a Google Ads tool, and not replacing yourself.

title: Weekly 42: How the Content Board Works
description: The flow behind the Workbench content Kanban, in more detail than you wanted. Five columns that are five folders, so dragging a card physically moves the markdown file. Ideas harvested overnight and scored out of 100 (threshold pushed from 70 to 85, because 25 ideas means reading none). Dragging to Draft spawns a colour-tinted terminal. Then the QA stack that accreted over time - scaffolding scan, reader's-eyes check, six separate evals - and rules written from the diff between what it wrote and what Mike changed.

title: Monthly Q&A: June 2026
description: The six-level trust progression that replaces the old five-step model, with Level 4 Systems as the month's goal - wiring skills, context and data together, plus the observability and logging that make a system worth trusting. The free Agency Brain launch with owner, scout and team-member roles. The Google Ads Proxy course that moves API keys into a Cloudflare Worker and saves big reports as CSVs so they never fill the context window. And why HTML beats Markdown for anything you want to review or edit.
